explain.say: Could you write rules to tell a cat from a dog? Pointy ears? Some dogs have those. Whiskers? Dogs too! Rules get messy, so instead we let the computer learn from examples. This is machine learning. Look at the first step: show it thousands of labelled photos.

explain.say: Look at the next step. The computer, called a model, looks at a photo and makes a guess: cat! At first its guesses are random, like a baby pointing at animals. What do you think we do next?

explain.say: We check the label. If the photo really was a dog, the guess was wrong. So look at the last step: the model adjusts its inside numbers a tiny bit, so that next time it is a little more likely to be right. Then round again! How is that like you learning to ride a bike?

explain.say: After thousands of rounds, look how the line climbs. Correct guesses rise fast at first, then level off near the top. It never quite reaches perfect. Can you spot where it slows down?

Brilliant! One warning: a model only knows its examples. Shown only big dogs, it may call a tiny chihuahua a cat! So people must choose fair, varied examples. Wow fact: the famous ImageNet collection has over 14 million labelled pictures for training. Challenge: what examples would teach it to spot a mango?

faq.a: Training data is the set of examples a machine learning model learns from, such as thousands of photos each labelled cat or dog. Better and more varied examples make a better model.
asks: What does an AI learn from?

faq.q: How does a machine learn from mistakes?
faq.a: After each guess, the model compares it with the right answer and nudges its internal numbers, called weights, to make the right answer a little more likely next time. Repeating this millions of times makes it accurate.
asks: What happens when the model is wrong?

faq.a: Machine learning is a way of making computers do tasks by learning patterns from examples, instead of a person writing every rule by hand.
asks: How is machine learning different from normal programming?

faq.a: Yes. A model can be wrong when it meets something unlike its training examples, and it can copy unfairness from its examples. That is why people check and test AI.
It sorts photos on your phone, suggests videos, translates languages, helps doctors spot disease on scans, and filters spam email.
asks: Do I use AI every day?

facts: The ImageNet dataset contains more than 14 million hand-labelled images.
A machine learning model improves by adjusting internal numbers called weights to reduce its errors on training examples.

quiz.say: A model was trained only on photos of black cats. It sees a ginger cat. What might happen?
quiz.show: Trained only on black cats, the model sees a ginger cat…
quiz.why: A model only learns from its examples, so something new can fool it.

wrong.1: It never saw a ginger cat, so it cannot be sure.
wrong.2: Models always give a guess; the guess may just be wrong.

quiz.say: What does the model do after a wrong guess during training?
quiz.show: After a wrong guess the model…
quiz.why: Small adjustments after each mistake are how it improves.

wrong.1: The photo stays; mistakes are useful for learning.
wrong.2: Mistakes are exactly what training learns from.
